title: Given a `List<Employee>`, produce a `Map<String, List<String>>` of department to the list of employee names in that department, using `groupingBy` with a `Collectors.mapping` downstream.
shortTitle: Group employees by department, then collect only employee names per department using Collectors.mapping
keyPoints: Collectors.mapping(mapper, downstream) transforms each element before the downstream collector stores it.
As a groupingBy downstream, mapping(Employee::getName, toList()) keeps the grouping on the full object but stores only the name.
The result type is Map<String, List<String>>: department key to a list of names.
Mapping the stream to names before grouping is wrong because it discards the department you still need to group by.
Swap the inner collector to change the shape: toCollection(TreeSet::new) gives sorted, de-duplicated names per department.
The classifier must never return null, or groupingBy throws a NullPointerException.
mapping does for a collector what Stream.map does for a stream, but it runs inside each group.

s1_definition.oneliner: `groupingBy(dept, mapping(Employee::getName, toList()))` groups by department but stores only the names, giving a `Map<String, List<String>>`.
s1_definition.profdef:
`Collectors.mapping` adapts one collector so that each element is transformed before it is stored.

- **Collectors.mapping(mapper, downstream)** – applies `mapper` to each element and feeds the result to `downstream`.
- **As a groupingBy downstream** – `mapping(Employee::getName, toList())` converts every grouped `Employee` to its name and gathers the names into a list.
- **Result shape** – the outer map is keyed by department `String`, and each value is a `List<String>` of names.
- **Why it is needed** – it keeps the grouping key (department) on the full object while reducing the stored value to just the name.
- **Composable** – the inner collector is free, so `toCollection(TreeSet::new)` yields a sorted, unique set of names per group.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya at the National Bank of India wants, per department, only the list of staff names, not the full employee cards. As each card drops into a department tray, she writes down just the person's name on a slip and keeps one slip of names per tray. The mapping downstream is her rule: before you store it, convert the card into just a name.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  List<Employee>
       │
       │  groupingBy(Employee::getDepartment, ...)
       ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  outer map keyed by department String         │
  │                                               │
  │   "IT" ───────────┐        "Finance" ──────┐  │
  │                   ▼                         ▼  │
  │   mapping(getName, toList())  mapping(getName, toList())
  │        │                          │           │
  │        ▼                          ▼           │
  │  ["Rajesh", "Amit"]      ["Priya", "Pankaj"]  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
       │
       ▼
  Map<String, List<String>>
```

```text
  How one element flows through mapping:

  Employee(Rajesh, IT)
       │
       │  classifier -> key "IT"
       ▼
  select the "IT" downstream container
       │
       │  mapper: Employee -> "Rajesh"
       ▼
  downstream.accumulate(container, "Rajesh")
       │
       ▼
  "IT" list now contains "Rajesh"
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
When Priya at the National Bank of India needs a department roster that prints only staff names under each department heading, she reaches for `groupingBy` with a `Collectors.mapping(Employee::getName, Collectors.toList())` downstream. mapping is an adapting collector: it applies a mapper to each element before handing it to the downstream, so inside each department group every Employee is converted to its name and the names are gathered into a list, producing a `Map<String, List<String>>` of department to a list of names.

The insight to always explain is why you do not simply map the stream to names before grouping. If you map Employees to names first, you throw away the department, and then you cannot group by it. `Collectors.mapping` solves exactly this: it keeps the grouping on the full Employee object and only reduces to the name inside each group.

The pattern is composable, which is its real strength. Swap `toList()` for `toCollection(TreeSet::new)` and you get sorted, de-duplicated names per department. Swap it for `joining(", ")` and you get a single comma-joined name string per department. The grouping stays the same while the stored shape changes.

The senior points mirror those of plain grouping: the classifier must never return null or grouping throws, and an empty stream gives an empty map rather than an error. Guard a possibly-null department by defaulting it to a placeholder like "UNKNOWN" before grouping.

Remember one sentence: `Collectors.mapping` lets you group by one thing while storing another, by transforming each element inside the group instead of before it.
